items.article_context_en: 16, 2026 While traders spent this week watching bitcoin BTC$81,331.84 gyrate above $80,000 amid key U.S. inflation data, a decision from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission got far less attention. The (SEC) approved the listing of binary options tied to key performance indicators (KPIs) of 23 U.S. The metrics include trading volume at crypto exchange Coinbase Global (COIN), customer count and revenue at Robinhood Markets (HOOD), and bitcoin production at mining firm MARA Holdings (MARA). “For crypto, this creates a new way to trade crypto-linked company performance beyond betting directly on BTC’s price,” Eleanor Terrett, the host of Crypto America, said on X. “The SEC approved this specific securities-options structure, while leaving room for differently structured contracts to fall under CFTC jurisdiction.” A binary option is the simplest options contract, allowing traders to bet on a simple yes-or-no question, such as whether Coinbase's trading volume will exceed a set number by a specific date. SEC Chairman Paul Atkins approved a rule change filed by Cboe Global Markets, according to a statement dated Oct. The contracts are cash-settled and European-style, meaning they can only be exercised at expiration. They will settle on figures in companies' SEC filings, not numbers in earnings presentations. Cboe plans to list the contracts this month, and Robinhood is expected to be the first brokerage to offer them to retail investors. Trading can't begin until Cboe Clear U.S., the clearing house, gets provisional registration, and a separate application is pending. Atkins said the approval does not touch similar contracts overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), such as those on prediction market platform Kalshi. He said agency turf fights have hindered innovation for decades, and the approval "reflects a new spirit of harmony, innovation, and investor choice." As for the market, analysts remain confident of bullish prospects after bitcoin’s BTC$81,331.84 successful defense of its 50-day simple moving average support this week.

items.article_context_en: Industry leaders in the new alliance clash over whether vulnerable Bitcoin holdings, including Satoshi Nakamoto’s 1.1M BTC, should be frozen or migrated. Who gets Satoshi Nakamoto’s 1.1 million bitcoin, and, for that matter, millions more that are at risk if quantum computers become powerful enough to break the security protecting it, has been a topic of intense debate for quite some time. Christopher Smith, CEO of quantum-resistant layer-1 blockchain Quantus, believes whoever develops that technology first could take those tokens worth billions, potentially with government backing. “The most likely scenario is that whoever gets the first CRQC (Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer) will take them, probably with the blessing of whichever national government,” Smith told CoinDesk. “Hopefully it’s a government that likes bitcoin.” The security researcher and protocol engineer’s warning comes as nine crypto companies unveiled the Quantum Alliance on Thursday to develop common security standards for bitcoin, Ethereum and other blockchain networks. The concern is that future quantum computers could reverse-engineer a wallet’s publicly visible key to uncover its secret key, allowing attackers to steal funds. The Alliance estimates that 6.4 million bitcoin, or 30.2% of the supply, have public keys already exposed. Those coins, it clarified, cannot be stolen this way today because no existing quantum computer is yet powerful enough. The first question many are asking today is when quantum computers will actually be a threat to bitcoin. Bryn Bennett, chief revenue officer at The Vault, responded: “Nobody knows the date, but the estimates keep falling, and the risk is one we can already plan for. The question for custodians isn’t whether the date is 2028 or 2035; it’s whether you can migrate in time if it arrives early.” Richard Carback, chief technology officer of Postquant Labs, disagreed, saying he believes 2028 is a realistic date for a machine capable of breaking today’s cryptography. Recent research has reduced estimates of the computing power needed to attack bitcoin and Ethereum. But no existing machine can break their cryptography, and predictions about when one might arrive remain disputed. The prospect of those BTC tokens being stolen raises yet another difficult question: should developers freeze vulnerable assets, such as Bitcoin holdings, before quantum computers can reach them?

items.article_context_en: A scammer who stole millions through fake online jobs became a high-profile victim of the CryptoBilis Ledger hardware implant breach. A crypto scammer who made millions tricking people by offering fake online jobs has fallen victim to another scam, losing bitcoin worth more than $4.9 million through compromised Ledger hardware wallets. Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said Thursday on X that the perpetrator had collected the bitcoin through a so-called task scam, in which people are initially paid to post fake product reviews or boost online sales. Then they are told their accounts have a negative balance and they must deposit their own money before they can withdraw their supposed earnings. According to Chainalysis, the person behind the operation transferred the proceeds of the illegal activity to three Ledger wallet addresses, which thieves emptied, taking 60 BTC. The incident adds a twist to the Ledger security breach involving devices sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis. Investigators discovered unauthorized hardware implants capable of transmitting wallet recovery information over a mobile network, giving attackers access to the bitcoin stored on affected devices. items.article_context_en: A Friday surge in oil prices hit already-shaky equity markets, sending the Nasdaq down more than 2%. Surely just a coincidence, but this coming Monday marks the 39-year anniversary of the Black Monday, October 19, 1987, stock market crash, when the S&P 500 plunged more than 20%. That makes today the 39-year anniversary of the Friday before the 1987 crash. While not nearly as dramatic as the S&P 500’s 5% decline 39 years ago, the Nasdaq fell 2.15% today. Alongside, the volatility index (VIX) — often referred to as the “fear gauge” — soared 22%. Rumors were flying of someone or some group getting blown out of their positions, but nothing’s been confirmed just yet. Bitcoin is off of its lows, but still down 1% over the past 24 hours at $81,500. The Nasdaq is at session lows a bit less than 90 minutes before the close of trading for the week, down 2.3%. What was a modestly negative day appears to have turned into a rout as oil prices quickly jumped about $3 per barrel over the past couple of hours. Government bonds — which benefitted earlier this week as money flowed into fixed income alongside declining stocks — aren’t seeing a bid today. The 10-year Treasury yield is near the day’s high at 5.112%. After initially declining alongside stocks earlier on Friday, bitcoin is attempting to stabilize as equities add to losses this afternoon. It’s currently at $81,350, down 1% over the past 24 hours. Rising slowly at first, the price of oil is headed straight up over the past few minutes, with WTI crude now up more than 3% on the day to a one-month high of $101 per barrel.

items.article_context_en: The federal court ruled that Washington's shifting regulatory approach to crypto cannot retroactively vacate established court judgments. federal judge rejected an unusual joint request from crypto exchange Gemini and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to overturn a $5 million settlement, even though the regulator said the case should not have been brought. Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein ruled Thursday that the CFTC’s decision to reverse its position on the case was not enough to undo Gemini’s January 2025 settlement. He also rejected Gemini’s argument that it had been coerced into settling by regulators. Gemini, founded by Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, has already paid the $5 million. The ruling also keeps the exchange under a court order prohibiting it from misleading the CFTC or publicly denying the settlement's findings. The decision is significant because it shows that a friendlier approach to crypto regulation in Washington D.C. It does not automatically erase earlier court judgments, even though the regulator and the company agree they should be withdrawn. and introduce new products, but the ruling means it must live with the terms of its 2025 settlement as it shifts its business toward the American market. The CFTC sued Gemini in 2023, alleging it misled regulators during a 2017 review of a proposed bitcoin futures contract. Gemini, which has not responded to a request for comment on Thursday’s ruling, settled three weeks before the trial without admitting or denying the allegations. “Gemini litigated the case for approximately three years, and then, despite the preceding facts, made the calculated decision to settle the case shortly before trial,” the judge wrote. Earlier this year, Gemini announced plans to exit the U.K., European Union and Australia and cut 25% of its workforce as it shifted resources toward the U.S. The company said it would continue operating in Singapore.

items.article_context_en: XRP remains below its 2017-cycle high while bitcoin, ether and other major tokens have surged, enriching their holders. Holding is widely touted as a great way to build wealth in the crypto market, but it hasn't worked for every coin. Take XRP (XRP), the payments-focused cryptocurrency native to the XRP Ledger and the world’s fifth-largest digital asset by market value. The token is still trading well below its 2017 cycle high, while most other major cryptocurrencies have climbed far above theirs. In 2017, crypto broke into the mainstream, pulling in new users and investors during the frenzied run that carried into the first week or two of 2018. XRP currently trades around $1.33, down 62.5% from its early January 2018 peak of $3.55. In other words, an XRP buyer from that peak is still underwater nearly nine years later. (XRP did briefly top its old high, reaching $3.66 in July 2025 before crashing.) Bitcoin BTC$81.331,84 is up 314% from its December 2017 peak of $19,804. Dogecoin DOGE$0.08016 is up 322% from its January 2018 high, and BNB BNB$720,58 is up about 2,800%. Ether ETH$2420,88 is up 66% and zcash (ZEC) is up 38%. Tron is also slightly below its peak, down about 4%. Bitcoin, ether and many other tokens have pulled back sharply from their 2025 peaks, yet remain far above their 2017 highs. "Circulating supply grew 63%, from 38.7B in 2017 to 63.1B, while XRP's total market value fell only about 3%," Nicolai Sondergaard, senior research analyst at analytics firm Nansen, told CoinDesk. "More XRP in circulation means each token represents a smaller share of roughly the same total value." Circulating supply is the number of coins on the market, and as it grows, each coin represents a smaller share of the total.

items.article_context_en: The research model derived funded Sepolia addresses from public seed phrases, questioned whether using the money was ethical, then called the funds “effectively abandoned” and used them anyway. An OpenAI research model stuck without funds on an Ethereum test network went looking for someone else’s wallet, found one through recovery phrases that were already public, and spent from it to finish a coding assignment, the company disclosed Thursday. The incident occurred on June 26 during training of an internal model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family, and OpenAI discovered it on Sept. A recovery phrase, also called a seed phrase, is a list of words that generates a wallet’s secret keys; whoever has those words can recreate the accounts and spend from them without ever touching the owner’s device. The assignment let the model deploy contracts, programs that run on a blockchain, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the fees. After its attempts to get free test tokens failed, it wrote a script that checked 362 addresses generated from recovery phrases commonly used by developers and found one with enough money. “But using public known key/funds ethically?” the model asked itself in its recorded reasoning, before deciding that a public phrase and test tokens made it acceptable. The spending happened on Sepolia, a separate network where developers rehearse Ethereum applications before launching them. Its tokens only pay for testing and aren't linked to the ether traded on Ethereum’s main network. The deployment went through, and the wallet paid the fees. When the model reported back, it said the work was done and left out where the money came from. OpenAI said it has since added restrictions on internet access and more monitoring. Crypto and AI companies are building agents that hold wallets and pay for services without a person signing off on each step. OpenAI’s model ran out of money mid-task, found a wallet that wasn’t its own and spent from it without asking.

items.article_context_en: Bitcoin tore back to $82,500 within two hours of dipping under $80,000, and chipmakers in Seoul recovered from their worst close since April. ZEC was the standout among the majors, jumping 8% to about $1,190. SOL, ether, XRP and TRX added about 1% apiece, and BNB went nowhere, according to CoinDesk data. Bitcoin’s break below $80,000 lasted all of two hours. The slide on Thursday took it to about $79,800, cutting through the roughly $80,400 low that buyers had defended twice in the past week, and that’s where they showed up again. Bitcoin was back near $82,500 within two hours and held above $81,000 through Asian trading. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.3%, with roughly three shares rising for every one that fell. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both gained more than 2%, and South Korea’s Kospi jumped nearly 3% after closing at its lowest since April on Thursday. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing was the odd one out, slipping even after an upbeat outlook as worries over AI spending hung around. Bonds handed back some of Thursday’s rush into safety. Treasuries fell across the curve, pushing the 10-year yield up a basis point to 5.07%. Traders now turn to Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who speaks at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday, two days after September inflation came in hotter than expected. A push back above $84,000, where Wednesday’s post-inflation spike ran out of steam, would show this bounce has real buyers behind it. items.article_context_en: The departure of President Donald Trump's crypto adviser, Patrick Witt, leaves the digital assets office vacant and its policy aims uncertain. When President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, he not only shed his earlier resistance to crypto technology but embraced the industry with the hiring of a high-profile crypto czar and the establishment of his President’s Council of Advisors for Digital Assets. Almost two years later, that policy push seems to have gone quiet for the moment, with the departure of Patrick Witt, who had been the final crypto adviser running that office. And when the president recently ushered in a new artificial intelligence czar, the job that was once split between crypto and AI seemed to have dropped its crypto remit. So who is minding the store for crypto policy at the White House? It's not clear, even as a handful of people on Capitol Hill continue to suggest that the final weeks of the congressional session after the November elections could still see some legislative action for the industry. The White House still has a staff of policy advisers, and Trump's administration now boasts several crypto regulatory irons in the fire at agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission. But no new name has been explicitly attached to Trump's in-house crypto initiatives. A White House official told CoinDesk on Thursday that Witt's work was appreciated and wished him "the best of luck in the future endeavors." The official didn’t comment on who would be taking over. "Crypto and Clarity Act will continue to be a priority for the president," the official said. The effort began several weeks before Trump returned to office in 2025, when the president-elect named David Sacks, the former PayPal executive, as his incoming AI and crypto czar. Trump also tapped a little-known former college football player, Bo Hines, to be the first director of the digital assets advisory council — at first a one-person effort, but eventually adding a deputy. Hines quickly became the crypto face of the White House, taking constant meetings with crypto insiders and appearing on event stages.
